name: Residence time
seoDesc: Residence time: work out residence time from the flow rate and the bed length. A free chemistry calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: The Residence time calculator turns the flow rate, the bed length and the inner diameter of the column into residence time. It suits a bench calculation involving amounts, concentrations or reaction ratios. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Residence time calculator work?
sections.html:
The Residence time calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports residence time in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the flow type); then you type in the flow rate, the bed length, the flow rate (2) and the inner diameter of the column.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• Pick the option that matches your case — 2 options, such as linear flow and volumetric flow. The choice changes which relationship the calculator applies, not just a multiplier, so it is worth reading the options carefully.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in centimeters per hour. The unit chip switches it to any of the 25 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in millimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in milliliters per minute. The unit chip switches it to any of the 39 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in millimeters. The unit chip switches it to any of the 34 supported units.
  • A measured quantity, entered by default in minutes. The unit chip switches it to any of the 27 supported units.

One field on this form is a choice rather than a number. Those choices decide which version of the calculation applies, so they are worth setting before you worry about the digits.

sections.title: The formula behind the Residence time calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Residence time=6 × bed length ÷ flow rate
Bed length=4000 × flow rate × residence time ÷ (PI × (inner diameter of the column ^ 2))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in minutes, and convertible to any of the 27 units on that chip.
  • Shown in millimeters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Speed, opening in centimeters per hour
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Time, opening in minutes
  • Flow rate, opening in milliliters per minute
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Length, opening in millimeters
  • Time, opening in minutes

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Residence time calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing a solution and checking the numbers first
  • Working through a stoichiometry problem
  • Converting between the units a protocol and your bench equipment use
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the flow rate, the bed length and the inner diameter of the column — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Residence time calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns residence time, derived from the flow rate, the bed length and the inner diameter of the column. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Residence time calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the flow rate, the bed length and the inner diameter of the column, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter flow rate in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Flow rate opens in centimeters per hour and the chip beside it offers 25 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Residence time calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
